coverage.notes: Absence claims in this pack describe one search, not the world: a listing of this course's folders in the student's iCloud term archive and his university OneDrive, in September 2026. All 11 weekly homework prompts survive, and each states the same grading rule, so the problem-set format and what earns credit are known from instructor documents. The 11 homework files are not bare prompts: each carries the student's own worked solutions, written by hand in digital ink on the prompt pages. An earlier pass read only their text layer and missed the ink. All 60 pages were read as images in September 2026. They show how the student laid out a solution, which the format block records as observed practice rather than a requirement. No page carries a grader mark, a score or feedback, so what the grader accepted is still unknown. One test paper and two keys are present as camera scans; an earlier pass counted two test papers. Those three documents were opened, under the student's explicit instruction, for exam SHAPE and for the method and presentation conventions the keys show, and for nothing else: no question, number, figure or answer from a real problem is recorded anywhere in this pack. The cheat sheets are the student's own and their contents stay out. No syllabus was found in either of the student's two archives as of September 2026. Methods now cover fourteen techniques, one per topic the prompts set: reduction, node and mesh analysis, Thevenin and Norton equivalents, capacitor and inductor relations, transients, phasor analysis, AC power, filters and resonance, op-amps, diodes, three-phase and safety, decibels and frequency ratios, and how a solution is presented. Eight of those rest on a prompt and a key together. Mesh analysis, transients, diodes and three-phase have no key; each now also rests on the student's worked pages, but only on the problems whose final value matches the prompt's listed answer, and each basis says how narrow that is. Nothing here covers the chapters the course reached after Test 2 in the instructor's own worked hand. The prompts' own text contains no worked solution, and the selected answers at the end of each are final values only. The lab has its own pack (engr204-lab). A lecture writing handout on audience, abstracts, graphing, and conclusions sits in this folder; it bears on the lab reports, and Test 2 carried a technical-writing short answer, so it reaches the lecture test too.

methods.title: Reduce a network to one equivalent between two terminals
methods.when: Any 'find the equivalent resistance seen between A and B' or 'find the equivalent capacitance' problem, and as the first move inside a larger problem.
methods.reading: Zekavat ch 3 (Resistive Circuits) for resistive combination; ch 4 (Capacitance and Inductance) for capacitors and inductors.
steps: Name the two terminals the equivalent is asked for. An equivalent is always with respect to a node pair, and the answer changes if the pair does.
Redraw the network whenever the drawing hides the relationships; the prompts give that as a standing hint.
Mark on the drawing which components are genuinely in series (the same current passes through both, with no branch between them) and which are in parallel (both ends on the same two nodes).
Write the combination symbolically with the components lettered before substituting any value, so the structure is visible and a wrong grouping is caught before arithmetic hides it.
Combine inward toward the named terminals, one stage per redraw.
For capacitors the rules invert: parallel capacitances add, series capacitances combine as the product over the sum. Inductors follow the resistor rules.
State the result with its unit, in the prefix the problem uses.
pitfalls: Calling two components in series because they are drawn end to end when a node branches between them.
Carrying the resistor rules over to capacitors without inverting them.
Answering for a different node pair than the one named.
methods.basis: The 11 homework prompts STATE the problems (find Req, find the resistance seen between two nodes, find the equivalent capacitance) and state the redraw hint in the instructor's own words. The Test 1 key SHOWS the technique: components lettered, the series and parallel groups marked on the figure, the combination written symbolically and then evaluated, and the capacitor rules written out before use. The key is a camera scan of handwriting, read by eye.

methods.title: Node voltage equations
methods.when: A circuit with several nodes where voltages are wanted, and any problem that asks for the equations rather than their solution.
steps: Choose a reference node, mark it, and name the unknown node voltages.
Write KCL at each non-reference node, taking every branch current as leaving the node and expressing it through the element that carries it.
Keep every term in the node voltages themselves; no branch current survives into the final equations.
Handle a voltage source between two nodes as a constraint between them rather than as a branch current.
Stop here when the problem asks only for the equations; the course sets that as a problem in its own right.
Solve when asked, then read the sign: a negative node voltage means the true polarity is opposite to the reference chosen.
pitfalls: Mixing assumed current directions between the terms of one equation.
Solving when only the set-up was asked for, or setting up when the value was wanted.
Writing an equation at the reference node as well, which adds a dependent equation.
methods.basis: Homework 3 STATES node voltage problems, including ones that say the equations need not be solved, and homework 8 states node equations written at an op-amp's inverting node. The Test 1 key SHOWS a set of node equations laid out, with the technique named before the algebra starts. Camera scan, read by eye.

methods.title: Mesh current equations
methods.when: A planar circuit where currents are wanted, or where the prompt names the mesh method.
steps: Identify the meshes and mark a mesh current in each, all circulating the same way.
Write KVL around each mesh; an element shared by two meshes carries the difference of their mesh currents.
Treat a current source shared between two meshes as a supermesh, with the source giving the constraint between the two mesh currents.
Stop at the equations when that is what was asked.
Convert a mesh current back into the branch current the question named, and state its direction, not only its size.
pitfalls: Sign errors on a shared element, which is where this method fails most often.
Reporting a mesh current where a branch current was asked for.
Giving a magnitude with no direction when the prompt asks which way the current flows.
methods.basis: Homework 3 STATES the mesh problems, including one that asks only for the meshes and their marked currents and one that asks for the direction of a current. No surviving key shows a worked mesh solution, so the presentation conventions here are carried over from the node method; that carry-over is an inference, not something a key shows. Also, for one problem only: a student's own worked page in the archived homework, whose final value matches that prompt's Selected Answers list. It marks each mesh current as a circulating arrow on the figure, lets a current source on an outer branch fix that mesh's current directly, writes the shared element's current as the difference of the two mesh currents, and states the direction of the result. A student page counts here only where its final value matches the prompt's listed answer, and no value from any page is recorded.

methods.title: Thevenin and Norton equivalents at a terminal pair
methods.when: A source network is to be replaced by its equivalent at named terminals, or a load is to be swept or matched.
methods.reading: Zekavat ch 3 (Resistive Circuits); with phasors, ch 6 (Steady-State AC Analysis).
steps: Name the terminals and remove the load, if one is drawn, before anything else.
Successive source transformation is the route the course's own worked solution takes: redraw the network at each stage, label the step, and carry the transformation toward the terminals.

Otherwise find two of the three quantities: the open-circuit voltage, the short-circuit current, and the resistance seen with every independent source deactivated (a voltage source shorted, a current source opened).
Combine what is left after deactivation by the reduction method to get the equivalent resistance.
Present both equivalents as drawn circuits with their element values, when both are asked.
Check the two against each other: the source current of the Norton form is the Thevenin voltage over the equivalent resistance.
pitfalls: Deactivating a dependent source. Only independent sources are deactivated.
Leaving the load connected while finding the equivalent resistance.
Giving one equivalent when the problem asked for both.
methods.basis: Homework 3 STATES the deactivation problems and the sketch that follows each. The Test 1 key SHOWS the full chain worked by successive source transformation, each stage redrawn and labelled, both equivalents drawn at the end, and the two forms cross-checked against each other. Camera scan, read by eye.

methods.title: Capacitors and inductors: relations, steady state, stored energy
methods.when: An energy-storage element appears and something time-varying or steady-state is asked about it.
methods.reading: Zekavat ch 4 (Capacitance and Inductance); ch 5 (Transient Analysis) for the steady-state substitution.
steps: Write the governing relation before substituting anything: current through a capacitor is C times the rate of change of its voltage, voltage across an inductor is L times the rate of change of its current, and the integral forms run the other way.
For a DC steady state, replace every inductor with a short and every capacitor with an open, say so in the work, and redraw before solving.
Stored energy is one half C times voltage squared, or one half L times current squared.
Combine several elements by the reduction method, remembering that the capacitor rules are the inverted ones.
Keep the prefix the problem uses and give the answer in it.
pitfalls: Applying the relation in the wrong direction, integrating where the derivative was wanted.
Losing the sign that comes out of differentiating a decaying exponential.
Using the resistor combination rules on capacitors.
methods.basis: Homework 4 STATES the relations, the steady-state problems and the energy problems. The Test 1 key SHOWS the convention of writing the governing relation first, the steady-state substitutions written out before the redraw, and the final expression boxed. Camera scan, read by eye.

methods.title: First-order transients, and classifying a second-order response
methods.when: A switch opens or closes and a voltage or current is wanted as a function of time.
steps: Find the initial value at the instant before switching, and carry across the quantity that cannot jump: a capacitor's voltage and an inductor's current are continuous through the switching instant.
Find the final value from the DC steady state of the circuit after switching.
Find the time constant from the network the element sees after switching: resistance times capacitance, or inductance over resistance.
Assemble the first-order form: the final value, plus the difference between the initial and final values, decaying exponentially with that time constant.
Recover any other quantity from the one just solved by KVL or KCL rather than starting again.
For a second-order circuit, classify the damping from the roots of the characteristic equation: distinct real roots are overdamped, repeated real roots critically damped, complex roots underdamped.
pitfalls: Using the resistance of the pre-switch circuit in the time constant.
Assuming a resistor voltage is continuous across the switching instant. It is not; only the capacitor voltage and the inductor current are.
Solving a second quantity from scratch when one line of KVL gives it.
methods.basis: Homework 11 STATES all of this, including the before-and-after instants, the derivations from a switched circuit, and the damping classification. No surviving key shows a transient solution, so nothing here rests on an instructor's worked example. It does rest, for four problems, on a student's own worked page in the archived homework, whose final value matches that prompt's Selected Answers list: the first-order form assembled from the final value, the initial value and the time constant; the values just before and just after switching given separately; a second quantity recovered from the first by KVL; and damping classified from the roots of the characteristic equation. A student page counts here only where its final value matches the prompt's listed answer, and no value from any page is recorded.

methods.title: Transform to the phasor domain and solve there
methods.when: Sources are sinusoidal and the circuit is in the steady state.
steps: Read the angular frequency off the time function first and write it down; every impedance depends on it.
Convert each source to a phasor in magnitude and angle form, and be explicit about whether the magnitude is an amplitude or an RMS value, because the course uses both.

Replace each element with its impedance: the resistance as it stands, the inductor as j times the frequency times the inductance, the capacitor as the negative j reciprocal of the frequency times the capacitance. Evaluate each on its own line.
Redraw the circuit in the phasor domain before solving it.
Solve with the same techniques as a DC circuit, now over complex arithmetic: reduction, dividers, node or mesh.
Give the answer in polar form with the angle in degrees, and convert back to a time function only when the problem asks for one.
pitfalls: Mixing amplitude and RMS between the source and the answer.
Dropping the j from a reactance, which turns a phase shift into a resistance.
Leaving a result in rectangular form where the course writes polar, or losing the degree mark on an angle.
methods.basis: Homework 5 STATES the phasor problems, including transforming a circuit and running node analysis in the phasor domain. The Test 2 key SHOWS the order: frequency extracted first, each impedance evaluated separately, the phasor circuit redrawn, answers in polar form with degrees. Camera scan, read by eye.

methods.title: AC power
methods.when: Real, reactive, apparent or complex power is wanted, or a power factor is to be found or corrected.
steps: Get the phasor voltage across the load and the phasor current through it, in the same convention; the course works these in RMS.
Complex power is the voltage phasor times the conjugate of the current phasor. Conjugating is the step that is skipped most often.
Read the parts off the result: the real part is the average power, the imaginary part the reactive power, the magnitude the apparent power.

Power factor is the cosine of the angle of the complex power, equivalently of the load impedance, and it is lagging for an inductive load and leading for a capacitive one. A power factor is never larger than one.
For maximum power transfer to a load, the load impedance is the complex conjugate of the source impedance.
To correct a power factor, place a reactive element in parallel with the load and size it from the reactive power that has to be cancelled.
pitfalls: Forgetting the conjugate, which flips the sign of the reactive power and turns a lagging load into a leading one.

Reporting an apparent power in watts, or a reactive power in watts. The unit engine cannot catch this: volt-amperes, vars and watts all carry the same dimension, and only the reader knows which part of the complex power was meant.
Reading a positive impedance angle as leading. A positive angle is inductive, and inductive is lagging.
methods.basis: Homework 6 STATES the real, reactive, apparent and complex power problems, the power-factor correction problem, and the leading and lagging hint in the instructor's own words. The Test 2 key SHOWS complex power written as the voltage times the conjugated current, the result given in both polar and rectangular form, and the power factor identified as lagging from the sign of the impedance angle. Camera scan, read by eye.

methods.title: Identify a filter, then find its corner, bandwidth and quality
methods.when: A circuit's behaviour against frequency is asked about, or a component is to be chosen for a target frequency.
steps: Identify the type by inspection at the two limits rather than by the topology's name: at zero frequency a capacitor is an open and an inductor a short; at very high frequency the reverse. Say what the output does at each limit, and the type follows.
For a first-order filter, the corner frequency is the reciprocal of the time constant, built from the equivalent resistance the reactive element actually sees, not from the source resistance alone.
For a resonant circuit, the resonant frequency is the reciprocal of the square root of the inductance times the capacitance.
Get the bandwidth from the resonant topology, and the quality factor as the resonant frequency over the bandwidth.
To choose a component for a target resonance, rearrange the resonance relation for that component and check the magnitude of the result against the values the course uses.
Sketch gain against frequency, marking the passband, the stopband, and the half-power point.
pitfalls: Using the source resistance where the equivalent resistance seen by the reactive element is meant.
Reading a frequency in hertz as one in radians per second, or the reverse; the course asks for both and they differ by two pi.
Deciding the filter type from one limit only, which cannot separate a band-pass from a band-reject.
methods.basis: Homework 6 and homework 7 STATE the corner-frequency, resonance, bandwidth and half-power problems, and ask for frequencies in both units. The Test 2 key SHOWS the limit reasoning written as two short lines before the answer, the equivalent resistance derived separately, and the gain curve sketched with the passband, stopband and half-power point marked. Camera scan, read by eye.

methods.title: Op-amp circuits under the ideal assumptions
methods.when: An operational amplifier appears and an output voltage, a gain, an input resistance or a bandwidth is wanted.
steps: Write the two ideal assumptions before anything else: the two inputs sit at the same voltage, and no current flows into either input. The course's own key opens with them.
Find the voltage at the non-inverting input, using a divider when a network sits there, and carry it to the inverting input by the first assumption.
Recognise the topology and apply its gain relation: inverting, non-inverting, summing, or difference.
When the feedback network is not one of those, write node equations at the inverting node and at any internal node, and solve for the gain symbolically first.
Input resistance is the source voltage divided by the current the source actually delivers, which is set by the resistors the source sees, not by the first resistor alone.
Closed-loop bandwidth follows from the gain-bandwidth product: gain times bandwidth is a constant for the part.
Check that the output sits inside the supply range when the problem gives one.
pitfalls: Assuming the inverting input is at ground when the non-inverting input is not.
Taking the input resistance to be the nearest resistor instead of the source voltage over the source current.
Using the open-loop gain where the closed-loop gain is meant, or the reverse, in a bandwidth calculation.
methods.basis: Homework 8 STATES the gain, bandwidth, superposition and input-resistance problems. The Test 2 key SHOWS the assumptions written out as a header line before any algebra, the divider step, then the topology's gain relation, and the input resistance taken as the source voltage over the source current. Camera scan, read by eye.

methods.title: Diode circuits by assumed state
methods.when: A diode appears and a current, a voltage or an output waveform is wanted.
steps: Use the model the prompt names, the ideal model or the constant voltage drop model, and say in the work which one is in use.
Assume a state for each diode, replace it with the model for that state, and solve the resulting linear circuit.
Check the assumption: an assumed-on diode must carry current in the forward direction, an assumed-off diode must sit under a reverse voltage. If a check fails, change the assumption and solve again.
For a waveform problem, work the input's two polarities separately and sketch the output over the input on the same axes, marking where the output clips and where it follows.
Report the model used alongside the answer, since the two models give different numbers for the same circuit.
pitfalls: Keeping a diode on when the solved current runs backwards through it.
Using one model where the prompt directs the other, or answering with one when both were asked for.
Sketching the output with no input drawn against it, so the comparison the problem wants cannot be read.
methods.basis: Homework 9 STATES the two models, directs which to use where, and sets the waveform-sketching problems. No surviving key covers diodes, so nothing here rests on an instructor's worked solution. One problem rests on a student's own worked page in the archived homework, whose final value matches that prompt's Selected Answers list: the diode assumed on, replaced by its constant voltage drop written on the figure, and the branch currents closed with KCL. A student page counts here only where its final value matches the prompt's listed answer, and no value from any page is recorded.

methods.title: Three-phase loads, and the safety calculation
methods.when: A balanced three-phase supply drives a wye or delta load, or a shock-hazard question is asked.
methods.reading: Zekavat ch 9 (Power Systems and Transmission Lines) for three-phase; the safety chapter the prompts cite for shock hazard.
steps: Identify the connection, wye or delta, and which quantity the problem gives, line or phase.
In a wye load the line voltage is the square root of three times the phase voltage, and the line and phase currents are equal.
In a delta load the line and phase voltages are equal, and the line current is the square root of three times the phase current.
Total power is three times the per-phase power. The factor here is three, not the square root of three.
Converting a balanced wye load to an equivalent delta scales each impedance by three, and the reverse divides by three.
For a shock question, take the current through the body as the contact voltage over the body resistance, and judge the hazard by that current, since the danger threshold is a current.
pitfalls: Swapping which of voltage and current carries the square root of three for the connection in hand.
Multiplying the per-phase power by the square root of three instead of by three.
Answering a safety question with the voltage when the hazard is set by the current.
methods.basis: Homework 10 STATES the wye and delta problems, the power problems, the wye-delta conversions and the two body-resistance questions. No surviving key covers three-phase. Every problem of that homework rests also on a student's own worked page in the archived homework, whose final value matches that prompt's Selected Answers list: the wye and delta line-to-phase relations written before the numbers, total power taken as three times the per-phase product with the power-factor term shown, the wye-delta conversion scaling inductance and capacitance in opposite directions, and the shock current taken as voltage over body resistance, each answer boxed with its unit. A student page counts here only where its final value matches the prompt's listed answer, and no value from any page is recorded.

methods.title: Decibels, octaves and decades
methods.when: A gain is to be given in decibels, or a frequency is to be moved by octaves or decades.
steps: A voltage or current ratio in decibels is twenty times the base-ten logarithm of the ratio; a power ratio is ten times it. Write which factor is in use before the number.
An octave is a factor of two in frequency and a decade a factor of ten, so move by multiplying or dividing, never by adding.
The midpoint of two frequencies on a logarithmic scale is their geometric mean; on a linear scale it is their arithmetic mean. The course asks for both and they differ.
Convert a decibel figure back to a ratio before using it in any arithmetic that adds or scales quantities.
pitfalls: Using the factor of twenty for a power ratio, or ten for a voltage ratio.
Treating an octave or a decade as an additive step in frequency.
Carrying decibels into ordinary arithmetic. The unit engine refuses the decibel outright for this reason: it is logarithmic, and adding two decibel figures is not adding the quantities.
methods.basis: Homework 6 STATES the decibel conversions and the octave, decade and midpoint questions. The Test 2 key SHOWS both decibel conversions written with the logarithm factor visible before the number, and the octave and decade moves written as multiplications and divisions. Camera scan, read by eye.

methods.title: How a solution is set out in this course
methods.when: Every graded piece of work: a homework set, and an answer on a test.
steps: Name the technique, or write the governing relation, before using it. Both the prompts and the instructor's own worked solutions open that way.

Show the substitution, not only the result. Credit here is for the shown attempt, and most homework final answers are printed in the prompt, so an unsupported answer earns nothing even when it matches.
Put the unit behind each quantity as it is written, not only on the last line.
Underline or box the final answer.
Mark the reference polarity or current direction on the figure when a sign convention is in play, and state what a negative result means: the true direction is opposite to the assumed reference.
Label a sketch's axes and mark on the curve the features the problem asks for.
Read back over the finished work for units, and for whether the method is legible to someone who did not write it.
pitfalls: Handing in a bare final answer. It earns nothing in this course.
Units only on the last line, or missing altogether; one test states outright that missing units will cost points.
Leaving an assumed direction unstated, so a negative answer cannot be interpreted.
methods.basis: All 11 homework prompts STATE the grading rule in the same words: credit is for an honest shown attempt, and work must be shown because the answers are given. Both test headers STATE their own presentation rules, one asking that work be shown clearly and the answer highlighted by underlining, circling or boxing, the other that units be placed behind quantities; both close by telling the student to check units and the clarity of the work, and one adds that missing units will cost points. Both keys SHOW the same pattern: the technique named first, the substitution shown, the final answer boxed or underlined with its unit. The keys are camera scans of handwriting, read by eye. The same order (relation first, substitution shown, final value boxed, the figure annotated with currents and polarities) appears on a student's own worked page in the archived homework, whose final value matches that prompt's Selected Answers list, in every homework where such pages exist. That is observed practice agreeing with the keys, not a further requirement. A student page counts here only where its final value matches the prompt's listed answer, and no value from any page is recorded.

magnitudes.quantity: power factor of a load in an AC power problem
magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: a power factor is the cosine of the angle between voltage and current, so it cannot leave the interval from zero to one whatever the load is. The bound is the definition, not a habit of this course's problems.
magnitudes.note: Above one: the apparent power and the real power were divided the wrong way round, or a reactive power was used where an apparent power belongs. Negative: the current phasor was not conjugated in the complex power, which flips the sign. The range says nothing about whether the factor is leading or lagging, which is the other half of the answer and is the student's to state.
